title: Hepatic Lobule Anatomy: Portal Triad & Sinusoid Vessels
description: Master hepatic lobule microanatomy, tracing dual blood flow from the portal triad across fenestrated sinusoids to the central vein and out bile canaliculi.
h1: Hepatic Lobule Microanatomy: Portal Triad, Sinusoids and Bile Canaliculi
blurb: Hexagonal liver micro-units where portal vein and hepatic artery blood flows inward across fenestrated sinusoids to the central vein while bile flows outward.
lead: Under the microscope, the liver is organized into hexagonal lobules where nutrient-rich portal blood and oxygenated arterial blood mix and flow past hepatocyte plates. In this illustrated guide to hepatic lobule and portal triad, we examine 20 documented structures—including portal venule, hepatic arteriole, interlobular bile duct, portal tract—linking regional topography, tissue architecture, physiological mechanisms, and clinical reasoning.
overview: Under the microscope, the liver is organized into hexagonal lobules where nutrient-rich portal blood and oxygenated arterial blood mix and flow past hepatocyte plates. The classical hepatic lobule places a central vein in the middle and portal tracts at its margins. Portal venous and hepatic arterial blood mix in sinusoids and travel toward the central vein, while hepatocytes secrete bile into canaliculi that drain outward toward portal bile ducts. Fenestrated sinusoidal endothelium borders the space of Disse; Kupffer macrophages reside in/along sinusoids and stellate cells in the perisinusoidal space. The hepatic acinus maps perfusion zones: zone 1 periportal receives blood first; zone 3 near terminal hepatic venules is relatively most hypoxia-vulnerable. Within the human body, the hepatic lobule · liver microanatomy (Lobulus hepatis · acinus hepatis) is situated in liver parenchyma: portal tracts at lobule periphery and central venule inside, receives arterial perfusion via portal venules and hepatic arterioles → sinusoids → central vein → hepatic veins, and is innervated by autonomic fibers accompany portal vessels and biliary tree; hepatocyte plates are not motor nerves.

The portal venule (Venula portalis) is small portal vein branch delivering nutrient-rich splanchnic blood to sinusoids. Physiologically, the portal venule feeds liver parenchyma. Structurally, the hepatic arteriole (Arteriola hepatica) comprises terminal hepatic artery branch carrying oxygenated blood. Physiologically, the hepatic arteriole governs adds oxygen to sinusoidal flow and supplies biliary structures. Structurally, the interlobular bile duct (Ductus biliferus interlobularis) comprises cholangiocyte-lined duct traveling with arterial and portal venous branches. Physiologically, the interlobular bile duct receives bile from canalicular/ductular route. Structurally, the portal tract (Tractus portalis) comprises connective-tissue region carrying portal venule, hepatic arteriole and bile duct plus nerves/lymphatics. Physiologically, the portal tract governs organizes inflow and bile outflow at lobular margin. Structurally, the central vein (Vena centralis) comprises terminal hepatic venule at center of classical lobule. Physiologically, the central vein collects sinusoidal blood toward hepatic veins. Structurally, the hepatic sinusoid (Sinusoideum hepaticum) comprises wide, discontinuous capillary channel between plates of hepatocytes. Physiologically, the hepatic sinusoid allows blood–hepatocyte exchange en route to central vein.

Clinically, regarding the portal venule, portal obstruction can raise portal pressure. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the hepatic arteriole, not the same as portal venous inflow. In clinical pathology involving the interlobular bile duct, duct injury causes cholestatic patterns. Medical evaluation of the portal tract also notes that triad diagrams omit additional vessels/lymphatics.

questions.question: How does blood flow through a hepatic lobule?
questions.answer: Branches of the portal vein and hepatic artery feed sinusoids near portal tracts; blood then drains toward the central vein. Structurally, the central vein (Vena centralis) comprises terminal hepatic venule at center of classical lobule. Physiologically, the central vein collects sinusoidal blood toward hepatic veins.

questions.question: Does bile flow in the same direction as blood in a liver lobule?
questions.answer: No. Hepatocytes secrete bile into canaliculi that move toward bile ducts in portal tracts, generally opposite the sinusoidal blood flow. The bile canaliculi (Canaliculi biliferi) is tiny sealed channels formed between adjacent hepatocyte apical surfaces. Physiologically, the bile canaliculi move bile toward portal ductules opposite blood flow.
